messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Hairdresser
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 54

She came to me six months after it happened, but she still speaks about it as if it were yesterday. Nineteen years old, a hairdresser at a busy salon in a strip mall near her parents’ house. She has been with her boyfriend since high school. She is petite, careful in her movements, her hands folded tightly in her lap during our sessions.

The story comes out in pieces. She had been working at the salon for about a year, just out of cosmetology school. One afternoon, a regular client came in for a color treatment. The client was in her fifties, chatty, someone who always brought homemade cookies for the front desk. My patient was mixing the bleach. She remembers the phone ringing, her coworking calling her name from the back. She looked away for a second. When she turned back, she grabbed the wrong bottle—a strong chemical relaxer instead of the gentle bleach she meant to use. She applied it to the client’s scalp without checking the label. Within minutes, the client began to scream. The burn was instant. The skin on her scalp blistered. Emergency services were called. The client was hospitalized for chemical burns over a large portion of her head. There was permanent scarring. Lost hair. My patient was not fired, but she was suspended for two weeks. She still works there, but now she only does blow-dries and trims—no chemicals. The salon owner told her she could earn her way back, but she never wants to.

She describes the weeks immediately after: not sleeping, replaying the moment under the fluorescent lights. The sound of the screaming. The smell. She cannot smell bleach without gagging. Her boyfriend tried to comfort her, but she felt he didn’t understand. She started to avoid the salon break room where the bottles are stored. She asks her coworkers to fetch things for her. She checks every label three times when she uses shampoo. She has dreams where she is the one burning.

Now, six months later, her life has shrunk. She works the quietest shifts. She stopped going out with friends. She cries every day, often without warning. A few weeks ago, her boyfriend touched her hand while she was chopping vegetables in the kitchen, and she flung the knife across the room. She apologized for hours. She constantly feels on edge, as if disaster is hiding around every corner. She told me she sometimes wishes she could disappear. She avoids mirrors. She avoids the client’s name if it comes up. Once, a woman with the same haircut walked into the salon, and she hid in the bathroom for twenty minutes, shaking.

Her family tells her it was an accident, but she cannot accept that. She believes she is a dangerous person. She describes a tightness in her chest that never goes away. She startles at the sound of a phone ringing. She cannot sleep without the television on, and even then she wakes up gasping, feeling the heat of that chemical burn on her own skin. She scored a 54 on the PCL-5. She came to see me because her boyfriend said he was scared for her. She agreed, but she said it mostly because she is tired of being afraid all the time. She is a hairdresser who cannot bear to touch hair color anymore. She is a teenage girl who feels ancient and poisoned. The story is still unfolding.
